Kobe 6 Total Orange – Rear Outsole Separation Issue

We’ve recently noticed a recurring issue with the Kobe 6 Total Orange: the medial side of the rear outsole tears and separates from the midsole.

Why Does the Outsole Separate?

Compared to other Kobe 6 colorways, many pairs of the Total Orange have a rear outsole that protrudes further beyond the midsole on the medial side.

During play, this protruding edge can catch on the floor. Repeated friction and impact can cause the outsole to tear at the edge and begin separating from the midsole.

What makes this issue worth noting is that we’ve observed it across multiple pairs of the same colorway, rather than on just one individual shoe. Based on this recurring pattern, we suspect that a structural factor related to the manufacturing process may be contributing to the problem, rather than it being caused solely by age or individual usage. However, a manufacturing defect has not been officially confirmed.

How Can You Help Prevent This Issue?

If you wear the Kobe 6 Total Orange, we recommend having the protruding edge on the medial side of the rear outsole carefully reshaped to follow the contour of the midsole.

Reducing the excessive protrusion may help minimize the risk of the outsole catching on the floor during play.

If the outsole has already started to tear or separate, it’s best to have the bonding condition and extent of the damage inspected before the problem gets worse.

A shoe’s durability depends not only on its materials and adhesive strength, but also on the shape and structure of its individual components.

At SHOERESTO, we look beyond repairing visible damage. We analyze recurring issues to identify their possible causes and help prevent the same problems from happening again.

✔ Material Differences: Zoom Uptempo 5 vs. Zoom Flight 5B

The Zoom Uptempo 5 was released primarily in versions carrying the “Premium” designation. The Premium version was upgraded with genuine leather in the upper. However, some areas such as the toe cap, which are exposed to frequent friction, use synthetic leather, so the entire upper is not made from genuine leather.

This combination of materials appears to have been designed with the function and durability of each area in mind. Synthetic leather is used in areas such as the toe cap that experience repeated friction and impact, while genuine leather is used around the vamp and side panels to provide greater flexibility and a more natural feel.

✔ The Zoom Flight 5B is different.

Depending on the retro release period and colorway, the Zoom Flight 5B can be found with both genuine leather and synthetic leather.

For older pairs, it is therefore important to examine the actual shoe rather than determining the material based solely on the model name or colorway.

One of the ways we distinguish the materials during restoration is by examining the bonding surface.

On pairs made with genuine leather, the bonding surface is often sanded as part of the original manufacturing process. On pairs using synthetic leather, however, the material cannot be treated with sanding in the same way, so the bonding surface is often left in its original condition before bonding.

As synthetic leather ages, it can develop cracking and surface peeling over time. Genuine leather, when properly maintained, is generally less prone to this type of surface cracking.

For this reason, when restoring vintage models, the choice of material can make a significant difference in the overall condition and restoration result.

Why Do Some Sole Reinforcements Require Sanding?

When working on shoes sent to us for sole reinforcement replacement, we sometimes find that the original outsole has been heavily sanded after removing the previously applied reinforcement.

So why is the original outsole sometimes sanded so aggressively?

The reason is not simply to increase adhesion. It is largely related to the characteristics of the adhesive being used.

Traditional rubber-based or CR (Chloroprene Rubber) adhesives often rely on surface abrasion as an important part of the preparation process.

In other words:

Surface sanding → Removal of contamination and weak surface layers → Creation of a suitable bonding surface → Adhesion

This process helps create a surface suitable for bonding.

However, heavily sanding the outsole can change its original thickness and shape. It can also create a level of wear on a brand-new shoe that makes the outsole look as though it has already been worn for an extended period of time.

That is why, for our sole reinforcement work, we use an adhesive system that does not require sanding, along with a separate surface-preparation process designed to remove contaminants and prepare the bonding surface.

Sole reinforcement methods can vary from one restoration shop to another. Different shops may use different adhesives, surface-preparation methods, and application techniques.

Before having your shoes reinforced, we recommend checking not only the finished result, but also what type of adhesive is being used and how the original outsole is prepared before bonding.

Understanding the process can help you avoid unnecessary damage to the original outsole.

At SHOERESTO, we do not sand down the original outsole. Instead, we use a separate surface-preparation process before applying the sole reinforcement.

✔Why Does Nike ZoomX Foam Tend to Delaminate?

Nike’s ZoomX is a PEBA-based foam material that offers excellent elasticity and energy return, but it is more challenging to bond than conventional EVA.

PEBA has a low surface energy, which makes it difficult for adhesives to properly wet and bond to the surface. This makes proper surface preparation particularly important.

In addition, ZoomX’s high elasticity causes the midsole to deform repeatedly during wear, creating continuous peeling and shear forces (forces that push the bonded surfaces sideways) along the bond line.

For this reason, some of the more recent carbon-plated running shoes use thermoplastic adhesive films, which are activated by heat to create the bond. However, depending on the type of film and bonding conditions, repeated flexing and contraction/expansion can also cause the bonding performance to deteriorate, and in some cases, delamination can occur within two to three years.

This does not mean that thermoplastic adhesive films always have a shorter lifespan than conventional adhesives. However, with highly deformable materials such as ZoomX, long-term durability can vary significantly depending on the type of film and the bonding process.

Ultimately, restoring a ZoomX bond is not simply a matter of choosing a strong adhesive. Proper surface preparation, the right adhesive or bonding material, and precise control of heat and pressure during the bonding process are all critical.

❓Why Did the Outsole Become Unusually Smooth?

Normally, as a basketball shoe is used over time, the outsole gradually wears down and the surface tends to become rougher from friction.

However, this pair was different.

When it arrived, the entire outsole was covered with a significant amount of dark, heavily adhered debris. After removing the contamination, we found that the outsole itself had an unusually smooth and glossy surface. 

A rubber surface becoming smooth and glossy through repeated friction, pressure, and heat can be associated with a phenomenon referred to as Glazing in the field of rubber tribology. Since this is not a commonly established term in the footwear industry, we would not classify this case definitively as glazing, but rather as a surface modification similar to glazing.

Could the Non-Slip Spray Be Related?

According to the customer, a non-slip spray had been regularly used on the outsole.

Depending on the type and formulation of the product, tacky ingredients may remain on the outsole surface and cause dust, court debris, and fine rubber particles to accumulate more easily.

In this case, a considerable amount of dark debris had become heavily adhered to the outsole.

We cannot conclude that the non-slip spray itself caused the rubber to change. However, it is possible that the combination of:

Non-slip product use → accumulation of contaminants → repeated friction and pressure → outsole surface modification

may have contributed to the condition observed on this pair.

After cleaning, the remaining smooth surface was lightly abraded. This significantly reduced the gloss and improved the slippery feeling of the outsole.

This case demonstrates that outsole traction can be affected by surface condition, not simply by the amount of tread wear.

We will continue to observe similar cases and share what we learn as we gather more information.
